Oct 13 : Daily Mirror publisher Reach said on Tuesday digital revenue remained under pressure in the third quarter, and that it remained cautious about the segment's full-year outlook as industry-wide disruption weighed on audience traffic from Google. • News publishers are navigating falling print readership and weaker referral traffic from platforms such as Google amid the rise of AI chatbots. • Google's AI Overviews, which answer queries directly in search results, have drawn complaints from publishers over falling traffic and advertising revenue. • Reach's revenue fell 14.1 per cent in the quarter, with digital revenue down more than 20 per cent .

Oct 13 : Anthropic said on Monday its experiments suggested small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.   • In its experiments, Anthropic looked at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help. • It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication. • However, the firm found that such AI models also struggled to complete the entire sequence from start to finish.

• In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication. • Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data center processors, Anthropic warned. • The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured. • The AI major also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after. • Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources. It added that systems should be strengthened to make it harder for such AI agents to spread.

Source: Reuters

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 12 : NASA's robotic Perseverance rover has now driven farther than any other vehicle on the surface of any world other than Earth, racking up 28.1 miles (45.2 km) since arriving on Mars in 2021, the US space agency said on Tuesday. The car-sized, six-wheeled rover reached the milestone 5-1/2 years into its mission to explore if conditions conducive to microbial life ever existed on Earth's neighbor. In doing so, it is visiting some of the most ancient terrain ever encountered in the solar system. "Perseverance's engineering hardware and instruments are in excellent shape with all redundant systems still available," Steven Lee of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, told Reuters.

"A recent assessment of all systems concluded that they are capable of operating well into the 2030s, likely beyond," added Lee, the project manager for NASA's two Mars rovers, Perseverance and Curiosity. Perseverance has exceeded the previous figure of 28.06 miles (45 km) driven on the Martian surface by NASA's Opportunity rover from 2004 to 2018. Both also exceeded the driving distances of any lunar rover. TRAVERSING JEZERO CRATER Perseverance, with its suite of scientific instruments, has focused on the Jezero Crater, a region in the northern hemisphere of Mars believed to have been flooded with water and home to a lake basin billions of years ago. The rover set the milestone in a journey toward an area called Idubi, through the region off the crater's western rim nicknamed Lac de Charmes. Its companion rover, Curiosity, rolls along in the Gale Crater near the Martian equator. Perseverance is showing no signs of slowing down, Lee added. Its mobility system mechanisms are being tested to show it can drive 100 km (62 miles) or more, he said, with the hardware to be tested to the equivalent of 150 km to 300 km (93 miles to 186 miles) in the effort. NASA attributed a major role in Perseverance's success to its self-driving capability, an autonomous navigation system called AutoNav. Lee said 90 per cent of its drives are done autonomously, with no human intervention. "Perseverance takes stereo images of the terrain ahead, generates a 3D software map, and selects the safest path towards a drive goal," he said. Another key component is the Vision Compute Element, a fast co-processor computer that allows the rover to process images and run its self-driving software very quickly, almost continuously during drives, Lee added. That contrasts with previous rovers, which needed to pause to "think" before each drive segment, he said. "Perseverance builds on the 29-year legacy of our past Mars rovers — Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity — each incorporating prior lessons and improving our ability to drive on another world," Lee said. POTENTIAL BIOSIGNATURE Lee said the rover's biggest achievement was almost certainly its discovery, unveiled last year, of a potential biosignature, or possible sign of ancient microbial life. This was found in reddish rock believed to have formed 3.2 billion to 3.8 billion years ago in a river channel feeding the lake that once filled Jezero Crater. The Lac de Charmes terrain, Lee said, may yield clues to early planetary geological processes, such as the effects of large meteorite impacts. Jezero Crater was formed by such an impact early in Martian history. Lee cited orbital evidence that some areas of the rim were once hydrothermal systems with warm or hot groundwater. "These areas may once have provided a warm, watery subsurface environment conducive to life," he added. "Indeed, some paleontologists hypothesize that life on Earth began in such environments." The rover's original mission envisaged just 12.4 miles (20 km) of driving. NASA recently approved an extension of its mission to explore the crater rim until roughly the end of 2028. The rover's plutonium-based power system is performing as expected, Lee said, adding it has "many years of useful energy still available."

Source: Reuters

TOKYO: Japan's cabinet approved three bills on Tuesday (Oct 13) to strengthen energy supply security, including measures to offset higher costs of importing crude oil through routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa said. The government plans to submit the bills to parliament during the current extraordinary Diet session. "Through these three bills, we aim to improve supply security by diversifying sources of crude oil and other fossil fuels and reducing related risks," Akazawa told a press conference. The bills include measures to diversify crude oil and other fuel procurement, provide transport insurance support and amend the law governing the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC).

The procurement diversification bill would create a grant programme to compensate importers for higher transportation costs when sourcing crude oil and fuels via alternative routes that avoid certain chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz. The scheme would be fully funded by contributions from a broad range of importers, including oil refiners, traders and petrochemical manufacturers. The insurance bill would allow the government to cover part of insurance payouts for oil tankers and other vessels carrying petroleum products and liquefied natural gas if foreign reinsurers are unable to provide coverage due to heightened geopolitical tensions, an industry ministry official said. The JOGMEC amendments would allow the state-backed agency to invest in infrastructure needed to secure alternative supply routes, including pipelines. Japan sourced 94 per cent of its crude oil imports from the Middle East in 2025, with 93 per cent of those shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz. In August, Japan unveiled a comprehensive plan to strengthen the energy supply resilience, with specific measures, including legislative steps, expected to be finalised by year-end. Crude oil procurement for October is expected to reach about 100 per cent of the average monthly supply in 2025, securing the necessary volumes of crude oil and petroleum products, Akazawa said.

AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says

The IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July.

FAST

BANGKOK: The global economy will still manage to top 3 per cent real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday. Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above US$100 a barrel , the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July. The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5 per cent. For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4 per cent global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage points from April.

The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week. "The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience." She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices. Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5 per cent this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on. The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95 per cent of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April. Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47 per cent of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains. Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran , with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3 per cent this year compared with the 1.7 per cent growth predicted in July. Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6 per cent, 16 per cent, 16.7 per cent, 15.6 per cent and 3.9 per cent, respectively.

Related:

WTO lifts global trade outlook as AI boom powers Asian growth

WTO warns of 'most serious and sustained' trade disruptions

UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content. Eurozone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1 per cent from 0.9 per cent in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defence spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage points from July to 1.3 per cent due to larger AI investment. The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5 per cent for 2026 and 4.0 per cent for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports. India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment. The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7 per cent in 2026 and 4.1 per cent for 2027.

Related:

AI productivity gains may not curb inflation, IMF's Tenreyro warns

AI is creating an economy that can grow without needing more workers. Should we be worried?

ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of US$96 per barrel for 2026 and US$87 in 2027. But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to US$130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2 per cent. AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6 per cent by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China. But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialise, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8 per cent directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4 per cent by 2028. This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1 per cent by 2028, including a 1.8 per cent drop in US output. The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels - advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.

Source: Reuters/ec

FAST

NEW YORK: The International Monetary Fund trimmed its growth forecasts for Latin America and the Caribbean for this year and next and said most of the region was getting little lift from the artificial intelligence boom that has helped other economies absorb the energy shock from the Middle East war. In its World Economic Outlook, released early on Tuesday (Oct 13) in Bangkok, the Fund projected regional growth of 2.3 per cent this year. That is down from 2.5 per cent growth in 2025 and from its July forecast of 2.4 per cent growth for 2026. The IMF cut its 2027 forecast to 2.5 per cent from 2.7 per cent. The regional downgrades come even as the Fund nudged up its world growth forecast for this year to 3.1 per cent from July's 3.0 per cent, crediting rerouted energy supplies and AI-driven investment for the resilience of what it calls a split global economy. The Middle East war has turned energy into a global inflation shock, with Brent crude about 45 per cent above its prewar level. Higher fuel and power costs are squeezing households and businesses, while fears of persistent inflation have helped push global borrowing costs to multidecade highs.

In Latin America, the IMF said, the energy shock's effect depends on whether gains for commodity exporters outweigh losses for energy importers and on how credible central banks' inflation targets are, adding that "there is little offset from the technology upturn in most countries." Of the three Latin American economies the IMF listed separately in its July World Economic Outlook update, Argentina took the deepest cut in its output estimate. The Fund now expects Argentine growth to slow to 2.1 per cent this year from 4.5 per cent in 2025, well below the 3.5 per cent it forecast in July, and it lowered its 2027 forecast to 3.5 per cent from 4.0 per cent. The report shows inflation is forecast to fall to 32.5 per cent this year from 41.9 per cent in 2025. Brazil's forecasts fell to 2.2 per cent for this year and 1.9 per cent for 2027, from 2.4 per cent and 2.2 per cent in July, when the IMF had expected Brazilian growth to "remain resilient" this year. The Fund now expects growth to slow next year, citing still-restrictive monetary conditions aimed at bringing inflation back to target, the withdrawal of government fiscal support and global uncertainty. Mexico moved the other way, with its 2026 forecast raised to 1.5 per cent from 1.2 per cent. The Fund previously linked Mexico's expected pickup to less restrictive domestic policies. It now points to exports, including through AI supply chains, and to investment that is stabilising as growth quickens next year. Even so, it trimmed Mexico's 2027 forecast to 1.8 per cent from 1.9 per cent and said trade and other uncertainties would keep holding back activity. The report's tables show Chile's growth slowing to 0.6 per cent this year from 2.5 per cent, Bolivia's economy shrinking 3.0 per cent after a 1.6 per cent contraction in 2025, and Venezuelan inflation speeding up to 467.9 per cent from 252.0 per cent. The IMF said risks remain tilted to the downside. It warned that market turmoil could hit emerging economies through higher government borrowing costs, pressure on their currencies and tighter local financial conditions.

Source: Reuters

The International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday (Oct 13) the Bank of Japan will likely raise interest rates gradually "toward a neutral setting" despite an expected slowdown in growth, aligning with other central banks facing inflationary pressures. "Growth in Japan is projected to slow to 0.7 per cent in 2026, with fiscal support measures partly cushioning the impact from higher energy prices, and to stabilise at that level in 2027 as the energy shock dissipates and monetary policy gradually normalises," the IMF said in its World Economic Outlook. The growth forecast for 2026 follows last year's 1.2 per cent expansion. The IMF expects Japan's economy to grow 0.7 per cent in 2027. The BOJ raised interest rates to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent in September and signalled its readiness to keep tightening policy to forestall the risk of inflation overshooting its 2 per cent target.

Japan's heavy reliance on imports for fuel and raw materials makes its economy particularly vulnerable to the inflationary impact from the energy shock and a weak currency. Without singling out any country, the IMF said monetary policy can look through the direct and short-term indirect effects on inflation "only if the shock is temporary." Even where looking through the shock is deemed appropriate, central banks may need to raise nominal interest rates if inflation expectations heighten, to keep real borrowing costs steady, it said in the report. The report also said exchange rates have experienced high volatility especially in Asia, prompting intervention by some countries, including a joint Japan-US operation to prop up the sagging yen. "Maintaining orderly adjustment and financial stability is vital while large shocks are unfolding," it said. While economies should allow exchange rates to move flexibly to absorb external shocks, currency intervention becomes an option if market moves are disorderly, the IMF said. "Where (currency) depreciation becomes self-reinforcing, market liquidity evaporates, or currency movements threaten price stability through large pass-through or balance sheet stress, temporary foreign exchange intervention" can be considered, the report said.

Oct 12 : Oil prices fell on Tuesday and were on track for their first decline in nearly a week, as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia. Brent crude futures dropped $1.18, or 1.1 per cent, to $105.47 a barrel by 0625 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.17, or 1.3 per cent, at $92.57 a barrel. Both benchmarks climbed nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, with Brent settling at its highest since September 15. US President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.

Additional supplies could help alleviate tightness in global fuel markets, tempering some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices recently. However, "there is considerable scepticism over the Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, particularly with reports that Russia has hit Ukrainian energy targets since Trump announced it," ING analysts said in a note. Lawmakers from both parties in the US complained Trump's agreement with Putin appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport over the weekend, while tanker attacks were reported near the Strait of Hormuz. The incidents threatened to derail a recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, and have reinforced fears of further disruptions along one of the world's most important energy transit routes. "Fresh diesel supply from Russia and steadier Saudi flows are offering some relief, yet the market still looks more worried about the risk of further hits to ships or pipelines in the Gulf than it is reassured by extra barrels," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade. "Until we see clearer signs of de-escalation, the path of least resistance still leans higher," he said. Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels of over one-third of the commodity value, impeding efficient movement of crude oil and products. OPEC has revised down its oil demand growth forecast for this year to 400,000 barrels per day from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, in line with developments throughout the year, Haitham Al Ghais, Secretary General of the organisation said on Monday.

TOKYO: Japan's wholesale prices rose 6.8 per cent in the year to September, according to data released on Tuesday (Oct 13), slowing from the previous month but highlighting mounting inflationary pressure that keeps alive market expectations of a near-term interest rate hike. The data will be among the factors that the Bank of Japan will scrutinise when its board produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at this month's policy meeting. The rise in the corporate goods price index, which measures the price companies charge each other for their goods and services, compared with the median market forecast for a 7.6 per cent increase. It slowed from a 7.6 per cent gain in August. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5 per cent in September from a year earlier, the data released by the BOJ showed, a sign that the currency's weakness continued to push up the cost of raw material imports.

"Wholesale inflation will likely re-accelerate given strong uncertainty over the Middle East conflict, which is keeping crude oil prices elevated," said Masato Koike, a senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "But there's no sign of inflationary pressure accelerating sharply for the time being," heightening the chance that the BOJ will stand pat in October and wait until December to raise interest rates again, he said. A recent spike in wholesale inflation was among the factors that the BOJ cited as evidence of mounting price pressures behind its decision to raise interest rates in June and September. While the prices of farm products fell 13.3 per cent in September from a year earlier due largely to plunging prices for rice, a broad range of other goods recorded price rises, including processed food, electric machinery and telecommunications equipment, the data showed. Prices of chemical goods rose 13.3 per cent, plastic products increased 12.8 per cent and non-ferrous metals goods were up 40.2 per cent, a sign of the increasing cost firms were facing from the weak yen, the US-Israeli war on Iran and robust AI-related demand, the data showed. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has said the key to the pace and timing of future rate hikes would be the extent to which such upward pressure on wholesale prices spreads to consumer inflation, as well as how that could affect consumption. Recent data showed core consumer inflation in Tokyo, which is considered a leading indicator of nationwide price trends, accelerated in September at its fastest pace in 10 months. Sources have told Reuters the BOJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target, highlighting its readiness to raise rates again in the coming months. The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month, while signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target, raising the prospect of tighter policy. At the meeting on Oct 29 and 30, the BOJ will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts that will be closely watched by market participants for clues to the timing of the next rate hike. Many analysts expect the central bank to raise interest rates again by the end of this year.

Oct 12 : The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission. The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil's National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press. Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier this month, USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement. OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organizations, including the New York Times.

SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website. "Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist," Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times' head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement. Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33 per cent globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat. SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardize how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work.
